Package com.dfiles.service

Class TableConverter

java.lang.Object
com.dfiles.service.TableConverter
public final class TableConverter extends Object
Facade for the Convert feature: given raw input bytes, a text encoding, an input format (or TableInputFormat.AUTO to sniff one), and an output format, produces the converted result. Never touches whatever the bytes came from — a pasted string, a local file, or a downloaded URL are all read once into memory and the original is never written back to.

The actual parsing and writing is delegated to one small class per format (DelimitedTableParser, JsonTableParser, XmlTableParser, MarkdownTableParser, YamlTableParser, XlsxTableParser, SqlTableWriter, CsvTableWriter, TsvTableWriter, JsonTableWriter, XmlTableWriter, HtmlTableWriter, MarkdownTableWriter, YamlTableWriter, XlsxTableWriter); this class only resolves AUTO and dispatches to the right one, which is what makes every input format able to produce every output format without a dedicated code path per combination.

TableOutputFormat.XLSX is the one output that isn't text — use writeXlsx(com.dfiles.model.TableData) for it instead of write(com.dfiles.model.TableData, com.dfiles.service.TableOutputFormat, java.lang.String, boolean, com.dfiles.service.SqlDialect).

  • Method Details

    • detect

      public static TableInputFormat detect(byte[] rawBytes, String fileNameHint, Charset charset)
      Best-effort format sniff, used when the user leaves the input format on Auto-detect. Checked in order: ZIP magic bytes or a .xlsx name hint (XLSX is binary, so it's checked before anything is decoded as text), then a leading < for XML, then JSON's leading [/invalid input: '{@code {}, then a Markdown table's leading {@code |}, then a YAML-shaped {@code key:} or {@code - } line, finally falling back to CSV or TSV by whichever delimiter is more common on the first line.'
